In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the concentrations of the four first-line drugs in infants were generally within the proposed adult target concentrations, but the rifampin concentrations were too low, and further investigation is warranted.
isoniazid concentrations in infants were within the target range, and the pyrazinamide exposures were similar to those previously reported in infants.

isoniazid (INH) and pyraziniamide (PZA) concentrations in infants compared favorably with proposed adult target concentration, while ethambutol (EMB) concentrations were lower but comparable to previously published pediatric studies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current recommended doses of the first-line anti-TB drugs for children are safe and efficacious.
we have demonstrated that the current WHO-recommended dosing regimens for rifampin are not adequate in children less than one year of age.

the current recommended doses of rifampin, pyrazinamid, ethambutol and isoniazid in infants, are appropriate for the first two weeks of treatment but may be too low in the second two weeks of treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current World Health Organization (WHO) dosing guidelines for first-line tuberculosis (TB) drugs in children are not appropriate for the youngest age groups.
the pharmacokinetic data we obtained from the study were consistent with the pharmacokinetic parameters of the first-line drugs used to treat tuberculosis in adults.

the pharmacokinetics of the first-line drugs for tuberculosis in young infants (less than one year of age) were similar to those in older children and adults, and in some cases, the concentrations were even higher.
